title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: At the beginning of July, more and more disquieting reports about the war began to spread in Moscow. People spoke of an appeal by the Emperor to the people, and of his coming from the army to Moscow himself. Until the eleventh of July no manifesto or appeal had been received, so exaggerated rumors about them and about Russia's position began to go around. It was said that the Emperor was leaving the army because it was in danger, that Smolensk had surrendered, that Napoleon had an army of a million, and that only a miracle could save Russia.

The manifesto arrived on the eleventh of July, which was a Saturday, but it was not yet in print. Pierre, who was at the Rostovs', promised to come to dinner the next day, Sunday, and bring a copy of the manifesto and appeal, which he would get from Count Rostopchin.

That Sunday the Rostovs went to Mass at the Razumovskis' private chapel, as usual. It was a hot July day. Even at ten o'clock, when the Rostovs got out of their carriage at the chapel, everything was full of summer languor — that mixture of contentment and discontent with the present which is felt most strongly on a bright, hot day in town. There was the sultry air, the shouts of hawkers, the light, gay summer clothes of the crowd, the dusty leaves of the trees on the boulevard, the sound of the band and the white trousers of a battalion marching to parade, the rattle of wheels on cobblestones, and the brilliant, hot sunshine. All the notables of Moscow, all the Rostovs' acquaintances, were at the Razumovskis' chapel. Many wealthy families who usually left town for their country estates hadn't gone away that summer, as if they were expecting something to happen. A liveried footman cleared the way for Natasha and her mother, and as she walked beside her mother through the crowd behind him, she heard a young man speaking about her in a whisper that was too loud.
"That's Rostova, the one who..."
"She's much thinner, but all the same she's pretty!"

She heard, or thought she heard, the names of Kuragin and Bolkonski. But she was always imagining that. It always seemed to her that everyone who looked at her was thinking only of what had happened to her. Her heart sank. She was as wretched as she now always was in a crowd. Natasha, in her lilac silk dress trimmed with black lace, walked as women can walk, with more calm and stateliness the greater the pain and shame in her soul. She knew for certain that she was pretty, but that no longer gave her satisfaction as it used to. On the contrary, it had tormented her more than anything else lately, and particularly on this bright, hot summer day in town. "It's Sunday again — another week gone," she thought, recalling that she had been here the Sunday before, "and always the same life that is no life, and the same surroundings in which it used to be so easy to live. I'm pretty, I'm young, and I know that now I am good. I used to be bad, but now I know I am good," she thought, "and yet my best years are slipping by, and they're no use to anyone." She stood at her mother's side and exchanged nods with acquaintances nearby. Out of habit she looked over the ladies' dresses and disapproved of the bearing of a lady standing close by, who wasn't crossing herself properly but in a cramped way. Again she thought with vexation that she was being judged and was judging others. Then suddenly, at the sound of the service, she was horrified at her own vileness, horrified that the former purity of her soul was lost to her again.

A handsome, fresh-looking old man was conducting the service with the mild solemnity that has such an elevating and soothing effect on the souls of worshipers. The gates of the sanctuary screen were closed, the curtain was slowly drawn, and from behind it a soft, mysterious voice pronounced some words. Tears came to Natasha, and her breast heaved; she did not understand the cause of them herself. A joyous but oppressive feeling stirred in her.
"Teach me what I should do, how to live my life, how I can become good forever, forever!" she pleaded.

The deacon came out onto the raised platform in front of the altar screen. He held his thumb out, drew his long hair from under his dalmatic, made the sign of the cross on his breast, and in a loud, solemn voice began to recite the words of the prayer....
"In peace let us pray unto the Lord."
"As one community, without distinction of class, without enmity, united by brotherly love — let us pray!" thought Natasha.
"For the peace that is from above, and for the salvation of our souls."
"For the world of angels and all the spirits who dwell above us," prayed Natasha.

When they prayed for the warriors, she thought of her brother and Denisov. When they prayed for all who travel by land and sea, she remembered Prince Andrew, prayed for him, and asked God to forgive her all the wrongs she had done him. When they prayed for those who love us, she prayed for her own family — her father and mother and Sonya — realizing for the first time how wrongly she had acted toward them and feeling the full strength of her love for them. When they prayed for those who hate us, she tried to think of her enemies and of people who hated her, so as to pray for them. She counted among her enemies the creditors and everyone who had business dealings with her father. And whenever she thought of enemies and those who hated her, she remembered Anatole, who had done her so much harm. Though he did not hate her, she gladly prayed for him as for an enemy. Only at prayer did she feel able to think clearly and calmly about Prince Andrew and Anatole, as men for whom her feelings were nothing compared with her awe and devotion to God. When they prayed for the Imperial family and the Synod, she bowed very low and made the sign of the cross. She told herself that even if she did not understand, she still could not doubt, and at any rate she loved the governing Synod and prayed for it.
When he had finished the Litany, the deacon crossed the stole over his breast and said, "Let us commit ourselves and our whole lives to Christ the Lord!"

"Commit ourselves to God," Natasha repeated inwardly. "Lord God, I submit myself to Your will!" she thought. "I want nothing, wish for nothing; teach me what to do and how to use my will! Take me, take me!" prayed Natasha, with impatient emotion in her heart. She did not cross herself but let her slender arms hang down, as if expecting some invisible power at any moment to take her and deliver her from herself, from her regrets, desires, remorse, hopes and sins.
The countess looked around several times at her daughter's softened face and shining eyes, and prayed to God to help her.

Unexpectedly, in the middle of the service and out of the usual order that Natasha knew so well, the deacon brought out a small stool, the one he knelt on when praying on Trinity Sunday, and set it before the doors of the sanctuary screen. The priest came out with his purple velvet biretta on his head, smoothed his hair, and knelt down with an effort. Everybody followed his example, and they looked at one another in surprise. Then came the prayer that had just been received from the Synod — a prayer for the deliverance of Russia from hostile invasion.
"Lord God of might, God of our salvation!" the priest began, in the clear voice, not grandiloquent but mild, in which only the Slav clergy read, and which works so irresistibly on a Russian heart.

"Lord God of might, God of our salvation! Look this day in mercy and blessing on Your humble people, and graciously hear us, spare us, and have mercy on us! The foe who throws Your land into confusion and wants to lay waste the whole world rises against us. These lawless men have gathered together to overthrow Your kingdom, to destroy Your dear Jerusalem, Your beloved Russia; to defile Your temples, to overthrow Your altars, and to desecrate our holy shrines. How long, O Lord, how long will the wicked triumph? How long will they wield unlawful power?

"Lord God! Hear us when we pray to You. With Your might strengthen our most gracious sovereign lord, the Emperor Alexander Pavlovich. Be mindful of his uprightness and meekness, reward him according to his righteousness, and let it preserve us, Your chosen Israel! Bless his counsels, his undertakings and his work; strengthen his kingdom with Your almighty hand, and give him victory over his enemy, as You gave Moses victory over Amalek, Gideon over Midian, and David over Goliath. Preserve his army, put a bow of brass in the hands of those who have armed themselves in Your Name, and gird their loins with strength for the fight. Take up the spear and shield and rise to help us. Confound and put to shame those who have devised evil against us. Before the faces of Your faithful warriors may they be as dust before the wind, and may Your mighty Angel confound them and put them to flight. May they be ensnared when they don't know it, and may the plots they have laid in secret be turned against them. Let them fall before Your servants' feet and be laid low by our hosts! Lord, You are able to save both great and small; You are God, and no man can prevail against You!

"God of our fathers! Remember Your bountiful mercy and loving-kindness, which are from of old. Do not turn Your face from us, but be gracious to our unworthiness, and in Your great goodness and Your many mercies do not regard our transgressions and iniquities! Create in us a clean heart and renew a right spirit within us. Strengthen us all in Your faith, fortify our hope, inspire us with true love for one another, and arm us with unity of spirit in the righteous defense of the heritage You gave to us and to our fathers. Do not let the scepter of the wicked be raised up against the destiny of those You have sanctified.

"O Lord our God, in whom we believe and in whom we put our trust, do not let us be confounded in our hope of Your mercy. Give us a token of Your blessing, so that those who hate us and our Orthodox faith may see it and be put to shame and perish, and so that all the nations may know that You are the Lord and we are Your people. Show Your mercy upon us this day, O Lord, and grant us Your salvation; make the hearts of Your servants rejoice in Your mercy; strike down our enemies and destroy them swiftly beneath the feet of Your faithful servants! For You are the defense, the help and the victory of those who put their trust in You, and to You be all glory, to Father, Son and Holy Ghost, now and forever, world without end. Amen."

Natasha's soul was open and receptive, and this prayer affected her strongly. She listened to every word about the victory of Moses over Amalek, of Gideon over Midian, and of David over Goliath, and about the destruction of "Your Jerusalem." She prayed to God with the tenderness and emotion that filled her heart, but without fully understanding what she was asking of God in that prayer. She shared with all her heart in the prayer for a spirit of righteousness, for the strengthening of the heart by faith and hope, and for its animation by love. But she could not pray for her enemies to be trampled underfoot, when only a few minutes before she had been wishing she had more of them, so that she could pray for them. Yet she could not doubt the righteousness of the prayer being read on bended knees either. In her heart she felt a devout and trembling awe at the thought of the punishment that overtakes men for their sins, and especially of her own sins. She prayed to God to forgive them all, and her too, and to give them all, and her too, peace and happiness. And it seemed to her that God heard her prayer.
